title: Leaving everything
hookLine: an estate sale, strangers holding someone's favorite mug; Shantideva on what we leave behind
tomorrow: why confess to someone who already knows?

lines: WHY FIGHT OVER ANY OF IT?
cards: The estate sale opens at eight on a Saturday. Strangers drift through a house where someone lived a long life. Green stickers on the dining table.

A man turns a coffee mug over to check the price; it's chipped at the handle, the one somebody reached for every morning. In the garage, a box of tools sorted with real care, three dollars for the lot.
Two neighbors hold up the same lamp and argue, politely, over who saw it first. And upstairs, in a drawer, a stack of letters about an old family feud that nobody here has heard of.
Everything someone guarded, loved, or fought over, sold by the afternoon. So yesterday's question: if you leave it all behind, why fight over any of it?

teach.h: I WILL HAVE TO LEAVE EVERYTHING.
teach.b: That's Shantideva's question, almost word for word. In the confession chapter he says: I will have to leave everything and go.

teach.h: HARM FOR FRIENDS, HARM FOR FOES.
teach.b: But not understanding this, I did harm for the sake of friends and for the sake of enemies. Then he looks down the road. Enemies will be gone.
Friends will be gone. I'll be gone. Everything will be gone.

teach.h: LIKE SOMETHING SEEN IN A DREAM.
teach.b: Whatever I enjoy, he says, turns into a memory, like something seen in a dream. Notice what he does not say. He doesn't say love doesn't matter, or that friends are worthless.

He says harm done for their sake, or against an enemy, is the strange part: a lot of damage over things that won't come with anyone. The grudge is the clearest case. It feels like protecting something.
Look closely and it's guarding a lamp at an estate sale. That's the freedom inside the verse.

teach.h: SET DOWN THE FIGHTS, KEEP THE LOVE.
teach.b: Not giving up the people you love, but setting down the fights that won't come with you.

how: Reflection on impermanence is practiced across Buddhist schools; in the Mahayana, verses like these are often read slowly and turned over in meditation as a way to loosen grudges and grasping.

o: seeing you'll go without it all, so harm for it is pointless
running away from home to find yourself somewhere else
giving away every possession to live in a monastery

games.q: the verse, piece by piece — tap the pairs.
p: and go without any of it
becomes a memory, like a dream
guarding a lamp at an estate sale

s: the verse teaches that friends and family don't matter
it targets harm done for their sake, not love. keep the people, set down the fight.
Shantideva says whatever he enjoys turns into a memory, like a dream
that's the image he uses for how everything we hold slips into the past.
letting go of a grudge means pretending nothing happened
the verse doesn't erase what happened; it asks why harm someone over what won't last.

games.q: your brother borrowed your jacket and returned it with a stain. you've been cold to him for two days. what would Shantideva ask?
o: make him pay for cleaning, so it's fair and you can drop it.
keep the cold shoulder until he apologizes properly.
ask whether a jacket you'll leave behind is worth harm between you, and let it go.
games.why: Shantideva confesses harm done for things he'll leave anyway. the jacket won't come with either of you; the brother is the one who stays.

practice: Listen for one sound around you: a fridge, traffic, a bird, your own breath. Follow it until it changes or fades.
Now bring to mind one small grievance, and let it go the same way, without arguing with it, just letting it pass out of hearing.

wordCard.voice: Leaving everything: Shantideva's reminder that he'll go without any of it, so harm done for its sake makes no sense.

orig.note: Sanskrit: letting go, giving up. A common word for renunciation; the verse itself speaks of leaving everything behind.

carryVoice: Your line: I leave it all. Keep the people, set down the fight. Nine days in.

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 2.34-2.36 (leaving everything I must go; harm for friends and foes; all becomes nothing; like a dream, it becomes a memory)
